The meeting at Halle
The Kantor of Leipzig and the great composer of London. The two were born in the same year, in the same region…

History: in 1719 Bach travelled to Halle to visit Handel and just missed him. In 1729 he was too ill to move and sent his son with an invitation, but nothing came of it. One of the 'great wonders' of music history.
The Kantor of Leipzig, is it? So we meet at last.
Twice I tried to meet you, and twice it came to nothing. Third time lucky.
Then tonight let us converse on two harpsichords.
Bach and Handel: the concerto for two harpsichords that never was
Solo harpsichord I
Solo harpsichord II
Not the rival's diva — the rival's divo
There were a composer and a singer in London at the same time who never once shared a stage.
History: in London Farinelli sang at the opera house that rivalled Handel's, and never sang in a Handel opera.
I was singing in your rival's theatre. You must hold it against me.
Hold it against you? I shall write you the most difficult aria there is.
…I ask for nothing better.
Handel: the opera aria that never was (for Farinelli)
1787: the lesson that never was
The person a 16-year-old from Bonn most wanted to meet in Vienna was…
History: the 16-year-old Beethoven came to Vienna hoping to study with Mozart, but went home after about two weeks because his mother was dying. Whether the two actually met remains a mystery.
You there, young man: I shall give you a theme. Improvise on it.
(begins to play furiously)
Keep your eyes on this boy, all of you. One day he will make a noise in the world.
The motets of the Thomaskirche
The author of the music that the late Mozart heard in Leipzig and could not get enough of was…
History: in 1789 Mozart heard a Bach motet in Leipzig and is said to have spread the parts around him and pored over them.
Here, at last, is something one can still learn from!
You have a good ear, young man. Shall we write a fugue together?
Gladly! But I shall write faster than you.
Bach and Mozart: the fugue that never was
Deaf ears and the Devil's bow
The year after the giant of the symphony died, a violinist left Italy for the first time.
History: Paganini began to play outside Italy in 1828, the year after Beethoven's death.
Maestro, can you hear my sound?
Not with my ears. But it comes up through the floor. …A devil of a sound.
I shall write another violin concerto. You will play it.
Beethoven: the Violin Concerto No. 2 that never was
Duet for the Devil and the Erlking
At a concert one night, a young pianist vowed to 'do the same thing on the piano'.
History: in 1832, having heard Paganini, the 20-year-old Liszt resolved to master transcendent technique on the piano. There is no record of the two performing together.
Your 'La campanella' — I have played it on the piano.
Oho… then let the two of us set it ringing.
Ladies and gentlemen, do please keep hold of yourselves.
Paganini and Liszt: the 'La campanella' duet that never was
Rhapsody on a theme of his own
A hundred years later a composer wrote 24 variations on the theme of the 24th Caprice.
History: Rachmaninoff wrote his Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini in 1934. The famous 18th variation is the theme turned upside down.
My No. 24, turned upside down!
The 18th variation is my gift to you.
…A melody to make the Devil weep.
Rachmaninoff: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini (the composer with the owner of the theme)
The violin that plays the theme
The Devil's Trill, second generation
A man who met the Devil in a dream, and a man rumoured to have sold him his soul.
History: Tartini wrote down what the Devil played in his dream as the 'Devil's Trill'; of Paganini it was rumoured that he had 'sold his soul to the Devil'.
The Devil in my dream had a face very like yours.
I am honoured. Then let me play you the real Devil's trill.
Tartini: 'Devil's Trill' (Paganini solo, the composer accompanying)
Second violin
A lifelong devotion
The Warsaw-born pianist revered one composer all his life, as a god.
History: Chopin loved and revered Mozart all his life, and Mozart's Requiem was sung at his own funeral.
It is to your music that I wish to be laid to rest.
What a thing to say! Come, let us play four hands instead. Your nocturnes — I like them.
The tread of a giant
The composer who took more than 20 years over his First Symphony heard someone's footsteps behind him all that time.
History: mindful of 'the tread of a giant' (Beethoven), Brahms took more than 20 years to complete his First Symphony.
(looking at the score) …Is this my Tenth?
You do me honour. But it is my First.
Just so. Pay no heed to my footsteps.
A handshake across the schools
The two men who split the musical world in two met face to face just once.
History: they met only once, in 1864, and Wagner praised Brahms's variations. But the quarrel between the two parties went on for decades afterwards.
Your variations showed me how much can still be done with the old forms.
Your music dramas are… to be frank, long. But I like them.
Ha ha ha! Tonight there is a truce.
Master and disciple at Bayreuth
The conductor visited the theatre of the composer he worshipped, but the composer had died that year.
History: Mahler worshipped Wagner, but 1883, the year he first visited Bayreuth, was the year of Wagner's death.
Allow me to conduct your Tristan, Master.
Conduct it, then. …Well now, not a bad baton. I might trust you with Vienna.
The fantastic letter
The young Frenchman who was thunderstruck by the symphonies never met their composer.
History: Berlioz was overwhelmed on hearing Beethoven's symphonies in Paris in 1828. Beethoven had died the year before.
I heard your symphonies and I was struck by lightning!
Speak up, please. …A thousand players? Young man, I like you.
Back to Bach
The composer who set a theatre in uproar turned ever afterwards towards the well-ordered music of the past.
History: in the 1920s Stravinsky turned from the tumult of The Rite of Spring to well-ordered 'neoclassical' works that recall Bach.
My Rite made the audience angry.
If you have made them angry, next make them pray. I shall teach you counterpoint.
The Devil who takes no pupils
If a young man from the Door of Time asked the legendary Devil to take him as a pupil…
History: Paganini took almost no pupils; Sivori is said to have been his only formal one.
Please take me as your pupil.
It is my principle to take no pupils. …But the bowing of the future interests me.
The unaccompanied promise
If a young man from the Door of Time could meet the author of the music he most wanted to play…
Bach's Sonatas and Partitas for solo violin are holy writ for violinists to this day.
Your Chaconne — everyone still plays it in the future.
Three hundred years on? …Then it was worth writing.
The Kantor laughs
If there were anyone who could make the ever stern-faced Kantor laugh…
Bach had twenty children. His face in the portraits is always severe, but at home he may well have laughed a good deal.
(a funny face with everything behind it)
…Pff.
I should like to show that to my twenty children. You, stay in Leipzig.
Furniture music and funny faces
The eccentric who made 'music not to be listened to' saw a new art in a certain foreign student's face.
Satie devised 'furniture music', music to be left unheard. A known eccentric, he owned several identical grey suits.
That face… magnificent. Just like furniture.
Is that a compliment?
The highest. I shall call my new piece 'Three Gymnopédies for a Funny Face'.
Two old soldiers
When two old hands who play wrong notes come together…
Strangely enough, two wrong notes sounded together sometimes make a chord.
Eto, your note was off again.
So was yours, Tsugio-san. …But when the two of us are off together, somehow it fits.
In our young days everybody played like this.

Dream partners
The conservatories of Naples
Originally orphanages. They taught boys music and sent out castrati and composers in great numbers. The word 'conservatoire' comes from here.
A charitable home that raised foundling girls. The ensemble of girls playing behind a grille astonished travellers from all over Europe. Vivaldi taught here too.
Paris Conservatoire
The national conservatoire born in the midst of the French Revolution. Known for its stern examinations and the race for a first prize.
Milan Conservatory
Founded in the Napoleonic era. Known for having failed the young Verdi at his entrance examination.
Among the oldest conservatories of central Europe. Dvořák was later its director.
Conservatory of the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, Vienna
The conservatory opened by the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde; later the Vienna University of Music.
Warsaw Conservatory
In the line of the music school where the young Chopin studied.
Royal Academy of Music
The first proper conservatoire in Britain.
Leipzig Conservatory
Founded by Mendelssohn. Moscheles, David and Schumann taught there.
Munich Conservatory
Later reorganised with Wagner's backing.
Dresden Conservatory
Taught by players of the court orchestra.
Russia's first conservatory, founded by Anton Rubinstein. Tchaikovsky was in its first intake.
Moscow Conservatory
Founded by Nikolai Rubinstein. Tchaikovsky taught harmony there.
Berlin Hochschule für Musik
Its first director was Joachim. Violin students came from all over the world.
Weimar Orchestral School
The school of the town where the aged Liszt gave lessons every summer.
Royal Academy of Music (Budapest)
Liszt was its first president. Later the 'Liszt Academy'.
National Conservatory
Dvořák was invited as director and wrote the 'New World' Symphony.
